t:
Paragraph (3) of section 402(j) of the Public Health Service Act (42 U.S.C. 282(j)) is amended—
    (1) in the matter preceding clause (i) in subparagraph (C), by striking “the following elements” and all that follows through “520(m) of such Act:” and inserting “for each applicable 
clinical trial for a drug that is approved under section 505 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act or licensed under section 351 of this Act or a device that is cleared under section 510(k) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act or approved under section 515 or 520(m) of such Act, the following elements:”; and 
    (2) in clauses (i) and (iii) of subparagraph (I), by striking the term “drugs described in subparagraph (C)” each place such term appears and inserting “applicable clinical trials described in subparagraph (C)”.

fable.w: This section is a technical amendment that strikes and replaces wording about which clinical trials (for approved drugs and cleared or approved devices) are covered by the results-reporting elements. The tempting reading is that clinical trial registry provisions involve the public or sponsors, but nothing in this text provides for a comment period, rulemaking, hearing, advisory body, consultation with outside parties, or a right to sue. No party outside the federal government is brought into a federal decision.
fable.s: Paragraph (3) of section 402(j) of the Public Health Service Act (42 U.S.C. 282(j)) is amended

qwen_block.w: This section is a technical amendment to the Public Health Service Act, modifying the text regarding elements required for clinical trials. It does not establish any process for public comment, consultation with outside entities, advisory boards with non-federal members, or rights to sue. The changes are purely legislative drafting adjustments to existing statutory requirements.
qwen_block.s: Paragraph (3) of section 402(j) of the Public Health Service Act (42 U.S.C. 282(j)) is amended— (1) in the matter preceding clause (i) in subparagraph (C), by striking “the following elements” and all that follows through “520(m) of such Act:” and inserting “for each applicable clinical trial for a drug that is approved under section 505 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act or licensed under section 351 of this Act or a device that is cleared under section 510(k) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act or approved under section 515 or 520(m) of such Act, the following elements:”; and (2) in clauses (i) and (iii) of subparagraph (I), by striking the term “drugs described in subparagraph (C)” each place such term appears and inserting “applicable clinical trials described in subparagraph (C)”.

opus.w: This section only changes wording in 42 U.S.C. 282(j) so that the results-reporting elements apply to applicable clinical trials rather than to drugs. It does not require or allow consultation, public comment, rulemaking, hearings, advisory committees, or lawsuits by anyone outside the government. The underlying reporting duty may involve sponsors outside the government, but submitting required data is not taking part in a federal decision.
opus.s: by striking the term “drugs described in subparagraph (C)” each place such term appears and inserting “applicable clinical trials described in subparagraph (C)”
opus.b:
**Step 1.** The tempting reading is that this section concerns outside parties (clinical trial sponsors) submitting information to a federal registry, which could look like outsiders engaging with the government. That reading fails. The section is a technical amendment that rewords which trials the results-reporting elements cover. It creates no comment period, rulemaking authority, hearing, advisory body, consultation, or right to sue. Mandatory reporting of data is not participation in a federal decision.

**Step 2.**

qwen_chat.w: This section contains technical amendments to the Public Health Service Act regarding the elements required for clinical trial reporting. It does not establish any process for consultation, comment, or participation by outside parties (such as the public, states, or experts) in a federal decision. The text merely changes statutory definitions and requirements for manufacturers and the FDA, which are internal regulatory matters.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that amending the requirements for clinical trials involves public participation because clinical trials involve patients (the public). However, the text itself only describes technical amendments to statutory language regarding what elements must be included in reports or records. It does not establish a process for the public to consult with the government, comment on rules, or participate in decision-making. The actors involved in the amendment process are Congress and the FDA (federal agencies), and the subject matter is regulatory compliance for manufacturers. There is no mechanism described here for outside parties to influence the decision.
